sponsors.name: Fractile
sponsors.what_they_build_technically: UK inference-chip startup (founded summer 2022 per fractile.com). Public descriptions: in-memory-compute accelerator for transformer inference, targeting decode latency (thousands of tokens/s) for very large models and long contexts. Early design (2024 to 2025 coverage): matrix-vector multiplies inside SRAM cells beside compute logic, RISC-V based, 'relatively advanced process technology but not bleeding edge FinFET'. Later interviews (BigGo summaries of No Priors/20VC podcasts) say it pivoted from SRAM-only (Groq/Cerebras family) because SRAM holds too little, to SRAM-class bandwidth attached to DRAM, claiming ~25x more bandwidth per chip than HBM parts, with a platform ramp aimed at 2H 2027. Sacra describes a PCIe card, custom ISA with RISC-V support, runtime with KV-cache management and paged attention, PyTorch/vLLM/SGLang integration, and a QEMU simulator for pre-silicon software work. Core thesis everywhere: inference is bound by data movement (weights, KV cache), not raw FLOPS. NOT public / not confirmed by me: analogue vs digital (Goodwin reportedly declined to say whether any analogue elements exist; one source names d-Matrix as the digital in-memory peer, which is not a Fractile statement), numeric precision (no source states INT8/FP8/FP4 etc.), process node, power, any measured silicon benchmark.
public_claims_with_urls: Raised $220M (Accel led; Pat Gelsinger angel/operating adviser), TNW dated 13 May 2026: matrix multiplications 'inside SRAM cells' next to compute logic; targets transformer inference (not training); metric 'watts per useful token'; claims 'up to 100 times faster and 10 times cheaper' than GPU setups, newer investor material '25 times faster at one-tenth the cost'; evidence so far simulation and small silicon only; first commercial chip not before 2027; Anthropic in early talks (not formalised). https://thenextweb.com/news/fractile-220m-inference-chip

2024 seed coverage: novel circuits execute 99.99% of the operations needed for inference in memory; initial targets 100x faster, 10x cheaper; target 20x the TOPS/W of any other system the company knows of; circuits work on unmodified leading-edge foundry processes; patents filed. https://semiconductor-digest.com/?p=27582

CEO interview: 'developing an in-memory compute (IMC) architecture for AI inference in the datacentre', using RISC-V and SRAM; 'a good portion of the chip is SRAM cells'; 'SRAM is not scaling aggressively'. https://www.eenewseurope.com/en/ceo-interview-walter-goodwin-fractile-ai/

Goodwin podcast summary: first chip SRAM-based, pivoted to high-bandwidth DRAM after about two years of work with memory vendors; ~25x more bandwidth per chip than NVIDIA/AMD HBM parts (a forecast, not a shipping product); single chip replacing work split across six to nine custom chips; ~150 staff; platform ramp 2H 2027; goal thousands of tokens/s for long-running agents. https://finance.biggo.com/news/9bea2d1aaa1ca2df

Company site: output 'at thousands of tokens per second', 'complexity and capacity challenges of operating large models at very long contexts', thesis that output latency will limit AI impact. No architecture, energy or precision detail on the page. https://fractile.com/

Sacra (secondary, company-stated figures): ~40 tokens/s on conventional hardware vs ~1,200 tokens/s on Fractile silicon; a month of continuous generation cut to about a day; first data-centre deployments targeted 2027. https://sacra.com/c/fractile/
sponsors.what_would_resonate: INFERENCE (mine, not sourced): Fractile sells the argument that decode is memory-bandwidth-bound and that latency per token, not throughput, is what long-running agents need. A result that would speak to them: take a real biomedical simulation or an agent loop, measure arithmetic intensity and achieved fraction of memory bandwidth on a GPU (roofline), show it is bandwidth-bound, and project what 25x bandwidth or in-memory compute would do. The dialysis-graft lattice Boltzmann workload (explicitly memory-bandwidth-bound) fits this directly; an AI-scientist loop whose wall-clock is dominated by serial LLM decode steps also fits their 'latency of long-running agents' thesis. Do not claim anything about their chip's precision or analogue/digital nature; nothing public supports it.
unverified: Analogue vs digital in-memory compute (not stated in any source I opened).
Numeric precision supported.

Whether the current design is SRAM-only or SRAM-plus-DRAM: TNW (May 2026) describes SRAM; podcast summaries describe a pivot to DRAM. Conflict not resolved; podcast statement is via a secondary summary (BigGo), not the audio.
The 100x/10x vs 25x/10x performance claims differ between sources; no independent benchmark found.
20x TOPS/W claim is from 2024 coverage of company statements.
Sacra's 40 vs 1,200 tokens/s figures and the PCIe/ISA/runtime details are a third-party profile with no model, batch or baseline stated.

sponsors.name: Callosum
sponsors.what_they_build_technically: London software company (founders Danyal Akarca, CEO, and Jascha Achterberg, CTO; Cambridge-trained neuroscientists). Builds an orchestration layer above hardware (not chips): splits a token-heavy workflow into subtasks and routes each to the model and chip best suited, aiming for lowest cost within scheduling constraints. Product name 'Tailored Inference' APIs, which let developers use task-specific combinations of compute without rewriting applications; two modes (best models on fast hardware, or Callosum matches workload to models, algorithms and chips). DCVC's partner post says routing examples include a frontier model on NVIDIA GB200 via AWS or open models (Llama 70B, Gemma 4 31B) on Cerebras wafer-scale chips, plus AWS Trainium/Inferentia. AI Engineer listing says workloads are translated into reusable functional blocks mixing deterministic operations with model calls, and the system learns how to route across configurations (a 'Principle of Maximum Heterogeneity' framework is named; I did not read its maths). Silicon partners named: Cerebras, Rebellions; Fortune also reports work with photonic networking companies. ARIA's Scaling Inference Lab lists Callosum as technology partner for Cluster 2, 'Heterogeneous Orchestration', deploying Q4 2026. How routing decisions are made is not public in anything I opened.
public_claims_with_urls: Fortune, 26 Feb 2026: $10.25M round led by Plural; ARIA gives grant funding for R&D on integrating novel chips (not an investor); routing 'each subtask of a complex workflow to a suitable model running on suitable hardware'; claims on complex multi-decision tasks of 2x accuracy, 7x speed, 4x lower cost vs identical hardware, company's own, no baselines described. https://fortune.com/2026/02/26/startup-callosum-cambridge-trained-neuroscientists-raises-10-million-venture-funding-orchestrate-ai-workloads-different-chips/

DCVC post by an investor (so not independent), 20 Aug 2026: $100M seed; first company to receive UK Sovereign AI fund equity; ARIA non-equity pre-seed; 'In one Callosum test, Llama 70B on Cerebras matched ChatGPT 5's accuracy at five times the speed and one-fifth the cost'; 'VMware of AI compute' positioning. https://www.dcvc.com/news-insights/dcvc-joins-100-million-seed-round-to-power-callosum-builder-of-a-new-orchestration-layer-for-heterogeneous-ai

Company site: Inference APIs that co-optimise models and hardware, combine 'diverse chips and compute primitives'; 'orders-of-magnitude' claims with no benchmarks or method given. https://callosum.com

sponsors.what_would_resonate: INFERENCE (mine): a result that shows heterogeneous routing paying off on a real scientific workload, with a measured cost, latency and accuracy per subtask. For this team that means decomposing the AI-scientist loop into stages with different needs (cheap fast hypothesis proposal, heavy reasoning, bandwidth-bound simulation, tiny-kernel evaluation), measuring each on at least two kinds of hardware or model sizes available in the event environment, and showing a router or scheduler that beats 'one big model on one GPU type' on cost-per-validated-result. Their scientific-workload evidence is thin publicly (examples are document extraction and computer use), so a biomedical workload is a new data point for them.

sponsors.name: ARIA (Advanced Research and Invention Agency, UK)
sponsors.what_they_build_technically: Funding agency, not a builder. Three research pillars: Charting the Course (software simulators estimating performance, power and cost of future algorithm, hardware and system-scale combinations), Advanced Networking and Interconnect, New Computational Primitives. Programme director Suraj Bramhavar (term-limited). Funded projects listed on the programme page are two simulator projects (Imperial/Edinburgh/Cambridge compute-graph simulator; Imec heterogeneous scale-out platform simulator); the page showed no funded projects under the other two pillars and nothing biology-inspired among them. top.title: Bits per Verdict: an AI scientist that finds the fewest bits its own conclusions need (merges H2, Bit Budget for the Heart, Bytes per Discovery, and a light version of H1's roofline)
top.description: One general engine, demonstrated on 2-D heart tissue with spiral-wave arrhythmia. An LLM planner proposes micro-LED light patterns that might stop the spiral, runs them in large batches on one GPU, and refines the best ones with Bayesian optimisation or evolution. Every conclusion it keeps (for example 'ring pattern P at irradiance I stops the spiral') then goes through an automatic precision check. The engine stores each state field (voltage, recovery variable) at progressively fewer bits, and adds analogue-style multiplicative noise, until the yes/no verdict or the threshold irradiance changes. The hardware result has two parts. First, a map of minimum storage bits and maximum noise per state variable at which the scientific answer still matches FP64. Second, the measured speed and memory gain from storing state in FP16 or BF16 on a bandwidth-bound stencil, plotted as dots on a measured bandwidth roofline. The chaos angle carries the novelty: single-precision cardiac trajectories are known to diverge quickly, so the test is whether the clinical verdict survives anyway. Stretch goal: run the same wrapper unchanged on a 2-D lattice Boltzmann (D2Q9) graft-junction flow to show generality.
top.scores: compute-hardware 4, AI-scientist loop and generality 4, biotech 4, visual 5, sponsor relevance 4, feasibility 4, honesty 4 (total 29/35)
top.verified: FluidX3D README (https://github.com/ProjectPhysX/FluidX3D): 'performance is only limited by memory bandwidth'; 153 B per cell-step at FP32/FP32 vs 77 at FP32/FP16; 93 vs 55 B per cell of memory; FP32/FP32 vs FP32/FP16S MLUPs/s are 17602 vs 29561 on H100 SXM5, 10228 vs 18448 on A100 SXM4 80GB, 5624 vs 11091 on RTX 4090 (ratios 1.68x, 1.80x, 1.97x by my arithmetic). Licence: 'Free for non-commercial use'. Lehmann et al. (https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.08926): FP64 vs FP32 difference 'negligible in almost all cases', 16-bit 'sufficient' for many. Marcotte and Grigoriev (https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1309.1720): arrhythmic cardiac dynamics with positive Lyapunov exponents 'become unreliable on very short time scales, when computed in single precision'. Optogenetic spiral control is established in silico and in vitro: eLife 2019 Attract-Anchor-Drag (https://elifesciences.org/articles/41076/figures), eLife 2020 sub-threshold drift (https://elifesciences.org/articles/59954), and 100% termination in CatCh atrial cultures (n=31) vs 0% in controls (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25082848/; search-snippet level). Klöwer et al. 2022 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9287017/): Float16 shallow-water model up to 3.8x on A64FX after rescaling and compensated summation. Prior art in precision tuning: Precimonious (SC13, https://www.davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/precimonious.pdf) and AMPT-GA for GPUs (https://engineering.purdue.edu/dcsl/publications/papers/2019/gpu-fp-tuning_ics19_cameraready.pdf) tune program precision against a user-set output-error threshold, not against a scientific verdict. NOT confirmed: that no FP16 or low-bit cardiac electrophysiology study exists (one search found none, https://arxiv.org/html/2510.12011v1 being the nearest GPU solver); FP16-storage speedup for a 2-variable cardiac stencil (bytes halve, so up to about 2x is plausible but must be measured); any Fractile precision or analogue/digital detail.
top.main_risk: A judge says '16-bit storage is known to work for LBM (Lehmann) and Precimonious did precision tuning in 2013'. The defence is that the unit of tolerance is the scientific conclusion in a chaotic system, per state field, with noise, found automatically by the engine. If the bit map comes out uniform the result looks dull, though it is still a finding. Formats below 16 bits are emulated (CPFloat or chop-style rounding), so they count for accuracy only and are never timed. Gaussian noise is not a calibrated device model, so never present it as Fractile's chip.
top.headline_metric: Minimum mantissa bits per state field (and maximum relative noise sigma) at which the termination verdict and threshold irradiance agree with FP64 in at least 95% of seeds, with confidence intervals. Measured cell-updates per second and percent of measured device-copy bandwidth at FP64, FP32, BF16 and FP16 storage, and the resulting bytes per cell (cells that fit per MB of on-chip memory, by arithmetic only).

top.title: Roofline-Gated Kernel Scientist (H1 + idea 2)
top.description: An agent rewrites a lattice Boltzmann blood-flow kernel for a dialysis graft join, trying memory layouts, fused collide-and-stream, in-place streaming and FP16 storage. A physics gate rejects any version that changes the answer (Womersley pulsatile pipe solution, mass conservation, wall shear stress against FP64). Every accepted version appears as a dot climbing a live roofline plot toward the memory-bandwidth roof. The speed it wins buys more graft designs in an outer search loop.

top.verified: FluidX3D reaches 85% of theoretical bandwidth at FP32/FP32 on H100 PCIe (11128 MLUPs/s) and 80% on H100 SXM5 (https://github.com/ProjectPhysX/FluidX3D). Agentic kernel optimisers exist: Astra reports 1.32x average on SGLang kernels (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.07506), STARK (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.16996), and an LLM 'GPU Kernel Scientist' loop that already uses that name (https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.20807v2, search snippet). The only LLM-on-LBM study found ran a CPU D2Q37 code and got small gains (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2503.13772, search snippet). Reward hacking is real: SOL-ExecBench flags 14.5% of agent submissions (search snippet, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.19173), and ProofWright says runtime tests can be masked by reward hacking (https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.12294). NOT confirmed: the ideator's '50-120x fake speedups, 3.13x to 1.49x' figures appear in neither 2511.12294 nor the Kernel Contracts abstract (https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.22032); a search attributes them to the Sakana AI CUDA Engineer case, but no primary source was opened. Whether the venue GPUs allow Nsight Compute counters is also unconfirmed.
top.main_risk: A chip designer learns little, because the optimisations are textbook and FluidX3D already reaches 80-85% by hand. If the agent plateaus at baseline-plus-a-bit, the headline is weak, and the graft loop adds build load without adding hardware insight.
top.headline_metric: Percent of measured device-copy bandwidth reached, baseline vs final kernel; number of physics-gate rejections, with a real cheat caught; graft geometries evaluated per GPU-hour.

top.title: Compute-Routing AI Scientist: surrogate, coarse or full simulation, and which lane (H3 + idea 3 + Solver or Surrogate)
top.description: An AI scientist designing dialysis graft joins chooses, for each question, a learned surrogate (tensor-core BF16 inference), a coarse lattice Boltzmann run or a full run, and the device lane for each. It is scored on full-fidelity-confirmed design improvements per GPU-hour and per joule, against full-simulation-only and surrogate-only baselines. It shows the overturn when the surrogate is biased.

top.title: Where an AI Scientist's Seconds and Joules Go (H4)
top.description: Instrument a complete AI-scientist loop running on a locally served open model. Measure the split of wall-clock time and GPU energy between LLM decoding, simulation, analysis and idle, on a cheap simulation and an expensive one. Then replay the trace at higher token rates to show when faster inference hardware speeds up discovery and when it does not.

top.title: Split the Heart: route the cardiac ODE and diffusion kernels to different chips
top.description: The heart-tissue solver has an arithmetic-heavy ionic ODE and a bandwidth-heavy diffusion step. Profile each, place each on the device that suits it, and give a per-kernel cost model, while an agent searches for light patterns that stop spirals.
top.scores: compute-hardware 3, AI-scientist loop and generality 3, biotech 4, visual 4, sponsor relevance 4 (Callosum, ARIA), feasibility 3, honesty 3 (total 24/35, ranked below 3 because the key hardware number is borrowed)
top.verified: Burchard et al. 2023 (https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physics/articles/10.3389/fphy.2023.979699/full), heart04 mesh, single device: A100 37.40 s total (PDE 27.34 s, ODE 10.05 s); GC200 IPU 76.57 s (PDE 19.75 s, ODE 56.82 s). The IPU's PDE win is attributed to its 47.5 TB/s aggregate on-chip SRAM bandwidth; the A100 SpMV reached at least 1507 GB/s against 1774 GB/s measured by BabelStream. The ODE loss is attributed to the GPU's floating-point throughput and the IPU's lack of caches and pipelining. IPU runs are FP32; the GPU precision in that table is not stated. An ideal split (IPU PDE plus A100 ODE, transfers ignored) is 29.80 s, 1.26x over the A100 alone (my arithmetic).
top.main_risk: Only GPUs are available, so any measured heterogeneous gain is likely zero or negative once transfers count, and the headline SRAM-chip number belongs to Burchard et al., not to the team. Their mesh is 3-D and irregular, unlike a 2-D stencil. Best used as one cited slide in rank 1's pitch (the bandwidth-bound half of heart simulation wins on an SRAM chip).
top.headline_metric: Measured per-kernel arithmetic intensity and achieved bandwidth; break-even per-step transfer cost for a split to pay off; Burchard's 1.26x ideal shown as a reference, not as a team result.

verdict.recommended:
Rank 1, Bits per Verdict, on the 2-D heart-tissue workload, with a roofline panel and a small time-and-energy panel from H4 built in. It meets all four constraints. Compute hardware: a measured precision-and-noise requirement per state variable plus measured storage-precision speed on a bandwidth roofline, which speaks to Fractile (data movement, bytes per cell on chip) and to ARIA's Charting the Course pillar (predicting performance and cost). AI for science: a general hypothesise, run, refine engine whose precision-falsification step wraps any array-based simulator. Biotech: optogenetic termination of spiral-wave arrhythmia, which the medical student can ground in published eLife and Cardiovasc Res work. Visual: a 2x2 wall of live spirals at FP64, FP16, emulated 8-bit and noisy, with a bit slider and a verdict heatmap that fills in as the agent bisects. It runs on one ordinary GPU.

Honest framing rules: time only native formats (FP64, FP32, BF16, FP16 storage); present emulated low bits and noise as accuracy-only; make no claim about Fractile's precision or analogue design; cite Burchard et al. for the SRAM-chip point, not your own runs; show an ablation of the LLM proposer against random and BO-only proposers, because SimulCost found LLM tuning slower than scanning.

Headline numbers to report, all measured on the day (none exists yet):
(a) Minimum bits per field for the voltage and recovery variables, and maximum noise sigma, at 95% or better verdict agreement with FP64, with intervals over seeds.
(b) Cell-updates per second and percent of measured copy bandwidth at each native storage format; the expected ceiling is about 2x for FP16 storage, as in FluidX3D's measured 1.68-1.97x for LBM.
(c) Bytes per cell, and cells per MB of on-chip memory, by arithmetic.
(d) Number of tempting speedups the verdict gate rejected.
(e) Share of loop time in LLM decode vs simulation.

Anchor numbers to quote with sources: FluidX3D 153 vs 77 B per cell-step and 1.68x on H100 SXM5; Marcotte's warning that single-precision arrhythmia trajectories become unreliable on very short time scales; Burchard's IPU PDE at 19.75 s vs A100 at 27.34 s.
verdict.plan_28h:
H0 is Sat 11:00; the event ends at H31, Sun 18:00. E1 = simulation and hardware engineer, E2 = agent-systems engineer, M = medical student.

H0-1 (all): ask the organisers which GPU model is provided, whether Nsight counters work, the API credit limits and whether a second chip type exists. Freeze the scope: 2-D Aliev-Panfilov or Fenton-Karma model, a light current added over a pattern mask, and verdict = no activation above threshold at time T.

H1-7:
- E1 writes a batched 2-D stencil in PyTorch or Triton with a storage-dtype parameter per field, chop-style mantissa rounding per field, and multiplicative noise injection. Spirals are started by an S1-S2 protocol, with a check that the spiral is stable at FP64.
- E2 builds the loop: an LLM proposes pattern hypotheses as JSON (shape family, timing, irradiance), a batch runner executes them, scoring is termination plus light energy, and BO or evolution refines. Every experiment's GPU-seconds and NVML energy go to a log.
- M picks the published sanity targets (a global pulse above threshold terminates; sub-threshold gradients make the spiral drift, per eLife 2019 and 2020), defines clinically meaningful verdicts and tolerances (threshold irradiance within X%), and writes the hypothesis-prompt context.

H7-12:
- E1 runs the bandwidth benchmark (device-to-device copy) and times cell-updates per second with CUDA events at FP64, FP32, BF16 and FP16 storage, then draws the roofline.
- E2 writes the generic precision-falsification wrapper (bisection over bits per field, then noise sigma) and starts the live dashboard (2x2 wall, bit slider, verdict heatmap, roofline dots, swim-lane time split).
- M checks that the simulator reproduces the qualitative published results and starts the pitch.

H12-20 (overnight): launch the campaign of many seeds and patterns. E1 turns on stretch work if ahead: D2Q9 LBM graft Y-junction (or XLB) under the same wrapper for generality, with E2 supervising the runs; drop it at H18 if not working. Sleep in shifts so one person always watches the runs.

H20-25 (Sun morning):
- E2 runs the ablations: LLM vs random vs BO-only proposer, measured as discoveries per GPU-hour.
- E1 computes confidence intervals, the bits-per-field map and the bytes-per-cell arithmetic.
- M writes the clinical interpretation and the 'where it fails' slide (ARIA asks for one).

H25-28: freeze the code, rehearse the demo with a pre-recorded fallback video, and prepare judge Q&A (Lehmann and Precimonious prior art, emulated vs native formats, no Fractile claims).

H28-31: buffer and judging. M presents the clinical story, E1 the hardware result and E2 the engine.
killed: H5 Designing living compute hardware: neuron-chip layouts are biological computers, not the sponsors' silicon, so there is no compute-hardware finding, and no published benchmark could be checked in 28 h.

Diverge Less (MCX photon transport): needs RT cores or Shader Execution Reordering, which datacenter GPUs probably lack (not confirmed for this venue). Its anchor papers (2608.21396, 2511.22779) were not opened, and rewriting MCX kernels in 28 h is too ambitious.

Bytes per Discovery as a standalone entry: 16-bit LBM storage is already shown by Lehmann et al. and FluidX3D, so alone it is a replication. FluidX3D is non-commercial and graft meshing is risky. Its bytes-per-cell idea is folded into rank 1.
Bit Budget for the Heart and H2 as separate entries: duplicates, merged as the core of rank 1.
Solver or Surrogate as a standalone entry: training a usable neural operator on on-site LBM data in 28 h is high risk and its arithmetic intensity is unmeasured. Merged into rank 3.
Two nested loops (kernel plus graft design) in one build: doubles the integration work without adding hardware insight. Only the roofline panel survives, inside rank 1.
Any projection of Fractile throughput, precision or analogue behaviour: nothing public supports it, and it would sink the honesty score.
